Precursor

pree-KUR-sur -- built on the root '-curs-,' meaning to run, with the prefix pre- ('before'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Precursor is a person or thing that comes before another, especially one that leads to or influences what follows.

Many historians view the printing press as a direct precursor to the modern publishing industry.

Worked Example

Long before smartphones existed, an early handheld device let people send short text messages and check basic email, paving the way for everything that came after it.

That earlier version that leads directly to something more advanced is exactly what a precursor is. Unlike 'copy,' a precursor typically comes first and influences what follows, rather than repeating it.

How Precursor Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

forerunner

forerunner: a person or thing that precedes and indicates the approach of another

predecessor

predecessor: a person or thing that came before another in a role or position

harbinger

harbinger: a person or thing that signals the arrival of something else

Antonyms

successor

successor: a person or thing that follows another

descendant

descendant: a person or thing descended from an earlier version

How Strong Is It? — predecessor → precursor → forerunner

predecessor vs. precursor

predecessor vs. precursor: Predecessor is a fairly neutral word for precursor -- predecessor often just names whoever or whatever held a role before, while precursor emphasizes that the earlier thing actively led to or influenced what came next.

forerunner vs. precursor

forerunner vs. precursor: Forerunner can feel more dramatic than precursor in some contexts: precursor is a broad, neutral term for anything that comes before, while forerunner often specifically signals or foreshadows something significant about to arrive.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of precursor.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-

prefix — pre-: before (Latin)

root — -curs-

root — -curs-: to run (Latin (currere))

suffix — -or

suffix — -or: one who or that which; forms a noun (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin currere meant 'to run,' and the suffix -or names 'one who or that which' does something. A precursor is literally 'one that runs before' -- arriving first and clearing the way for what follows.

Use the root in a new word: cursory

Use the root in a new word: cursory: He gave the report only a cursory glance before signing off on it.
